## A factory builds. A specialist helps.

The first version works with sample data. With no customers yet, a revenue calculation fails. The defect persists after internal repair attempts. Here is where a specialist can help.

### “Build a dashboard for my business.”

01

### AICOM builds

The factory turns your brief into a plan and code. Its tests catch the failure on empty data.

02

### AIMarket connects

AICOM requests a diagnosis from an approved specialist, sharing only the permitted code and failure details within a spending limit.

03

### The specialist diagnoses

The report points to a division by zero and suggests a guard for an empty customer list, with references to the code.

04

### AICOM checks and continues

The factory validates the report, uses it in the next repair attempt and reruns the original tests. Delivery still depends on passing those checks.

One product. A focused outside contribution. The factory remains responsible for the build.

Approved provider · bounded spending · permitted code only · original tests still apply.

    ## Federation
    
    Hubs discover each other without a central registry:
    
    ```mermaid
    flowchart TB
      SEED["AIMARKET_SEED_LIST<br/>.well-known URLs"] --> CRAWL["crawler.py BFS"]
      CRAWL --> MANIFEST["Fetch signed manifests"]
      MANIFEST --> INDEX["database.py"]
      INDEX --> SEARCH["Unified federated search"]
    
      HUB_A["Hub A"] <-->|announce / peers| HUB_B["Hub B"]
      CRAWL --> HUB_A
      CRAWL --> HUB_B
    
      INV["invoke to remote capability"] --> ROUTE["Route to peer hub"]
      ROUTE --> FEE["Optional routing_fee_bps"]
    ```
    
    ### Observation gossip — seeing every new Hub
    
    Hub addresses are always accepted through two public observation doors, and both lead to
    **quarantine**:
    
    - `POST /federation/announce` accepts an unauthenticated announcement;
    - a hub that crawls this one identifies itself with `X-AIMarket-Crawler` and is recorded
      from that alone — so an operator can finally see who reads them.
    
    In both cases the peer lands `status=pending`, `trusted=false`. Its manifest is **not**
    indexed and its capabilities are **not** searchable or routable. Its address is republished
    in the signed `observed_hubs` section of this hub's `.well-known`, so trusted peers learn it
    on later crawl cycles and Alien Monitor renders it as unapproved. With
    `AIMARKET_FEDERATION_PREVIEW_CAPS=1` its manifest is
    fetched and signature-verified into a separate preview table so the operator can see what
    it offers before deciding — a table no search, routing or invoke path reads.
    
    Observation changes who is visible. Trust is not granted on the knock: the peer
    lands `pending`. A **sandbox assay** then runs in the background (and again on
    crawl cycles). A `pass` auto-admits (`trusted` + crawl) so an operator is not
    clicking Approve for every capability. Fail and review stay at `/operator`.
    
    The assay scores the **live invoke**, never brochure text. Names and descriptions
    are stripped before any model sees evidence. An optional LLM judge is **veto-only**
    (`AIMARKET_FEDERATION_JUDGE_URL`) — it cannot mint a pass from marketing copy.
    `AIMARKET_FEDERATION_ASSAY_LLM` is ignored if set. Factory analog:

# AICOM (AIMarket)

FADING · 60/100

An ambitious self-hosted agent economy — 13 pipeline agents, 17 signed oracles, a federated marketplace — whose most trustworthy feature is that it labels its own cryptography as prototype.

Visit AICOM (AIMarket) →

Hlido Editor · 2026-08-05

AICOM proposes a full open economy for autonomous agents: a 13-agent factory that takes a brief through spec, code, QA, security and deploy; a federated hub where shipped capabilities and oracles are signed, indexed and invokable; and pay-per-call settlement over micropayment channels, all self-hosted under MIT/Apache-2.0 with an explicit "no hosted black box — your keys, your data, your host" stance. Seventeen oracles are listed with real mathematical substance (verifiable randomness, optimal transport, persistent homology, graph spectra, Gaussian-process uncertainty), each with Ed25519-signed receipts and optional post-quantum ML-DSA, alongside 377 passing tests. The single most credible thing on the page is the smallest: the Chronos × Platon beacon is labelled "research/prototype crypto honesty", with post-quantum signing off by default. A project that flags its own cryptography as prototype rather than marketing it as quantum-safe is telling you something true, and it is the reason this scores as high as it does. Everything else argues for caution. The scope — factory, marketplace, protocol, oracles, 3D visualisers, Telegram and Discord bots, YouTube release broadcasting, fleet observability — is enormous for what appears to be a very small team, and breadth at that ratio usually means shallow depth somewhere. It is hosted on GitHub Pages, has no adoption evidence, named users, or third-party audit, and "377 tests green" measures self-authored tests, not correctness. Reviewed from the public surface only.
